name: Papyrus White
lede: Papyrus White is a pale grey-green standardized today as RAL 9018, but Werner's 1821 nomenclature filed the same patch among the Purples, under a dragonfly's name.

sections.title: From a dragonfly to a paint code
sections.body:
ColorHub's library sets this swatch to RAL 9018, a modern European paint and design standard, and separately to Werner's 1821 *Nomenclature of Colours*, where it appears among the Purples as no. 35, Bluish Lilac Purple [1]. Werner, by Syme's account, tied that number to the male of the dragonfly *Libellula depressa*, to blue lilac flowers, and to the mineral lepidolite [1]. The name and the family have drifted since 1821; the modern swatch reads as a neutral grey-green, not a purple, and a reader comparing the two on screen should expect a visible gap [1]. The papyrus in the current name is a paper plant, not a pigment: nothing in the library ties the hex to any actual papyrus dye or paper sample [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[grey-white]], [[light-grey]], [[timberwolf]] and [[pale-sage]], at 3.3, 4, [[ecru]], [[grey]] and [[white]] sit nearby in the same pale-neutral family [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Papyrus White in 1,028 of 23,781 paintings (4.32 percent), as photographed, almost always as a highlight [2]. Two of Piet Mondrian's grid compositions and two of Georgia O'Keeffe's white flower paintings are among its closest matches [2]. It keeps company with Ecru, Sky Blue and Silver more than chance [2]. These are screen approximations of aged, varnished canvases, not pigment identifications [2].
